talks.title: Building The Right Business Culture To Manage Human Error by Ryan Pullen
talks.teaser: Provides building The Right Business Culture To Manage Human Error by Ryan Pullen and evaluates key implications for security practitioners.
talks.summary: Building business culture to manage human error in security.
talks.aiSummary:
Overview:
Ryan Pullen, Head of Cyber Security and shareholder at Stripe OLT, delivers a presentation at BSides exploring the intersection of organizational culture, human error, and cybersecurity operations. Drawing from experiences scaling a managed service and security operations practice through remote-work transitions, Pullen challenges traditional punitive security practices. He advocates for fostering psychological safety, modernizing cybersecurity hiring strategies, and aligning internal team incentives to significantly reduce detection and response times.

Key Topics:
- Cultural transformation of security operations during rapid growth and remote work adoption
- Reevaluating simulated phishing campaigns and transforming human error into an early-warning telemetry stream
- Challenging the "cyber skills gap" through non-traditional hiring and Simon Sinek's Performance vs. Trust Matrix
- Operational optimization: automating tier-one triage, cross-departmental collaboration, and shared team goals

Technical Details:
Pullen critiques legacy security awareness programs that treat simulated phishing campaigns as punitive human resource metrics used to discipline employees. He argues that penalizing workers who fall for phishing simulations cultivates fear and concealment, directly inflating an organization's Mean Time to Detect (MTTD) and Mean Time to Respond (MTTR). By pivoting the corporate culture toward psychological safety, employees are empowered to immediately report mistakes and suspicious emails without fear of reprisal. This transforms the workforce into an effective sensor network that accelerates incident response, enabling security teams to intercept the attacker's kill chain at its earliest stages.

Addressing industry hiring practices, Pullen challenges the conventional narrative of a cybersecurity "skills gap." He contends that rigid qualification barriers—such as multi-round interviews demanding rote memorization of Nmap command-line flags and mandatory degree requirements—artificially exclude capable talent. Applying Simon Sinek's Performance versus Trust Matrix, Pullen prioritizes high-trust individuals over low-trust high performers whose toxic behavior harms operational cohesion. His team recruited analysts from unconventional backgrounds possessing critical situational awareness and crisis-management skills, including ex-military personnel, paramedics, hospitality workers experienced in conflict resolution, and healthcare workers adept at explaining complex technical concepts to clients. In one example, a former scaffolder upskilling via TryHackMe was hired based on high motivation and client empathy. Operationally, this collaborative culture enabled internal hackathons that autonomously automated 29% of initial security triage and dramatically exceeded strict SLAs across 20,000 endpoints, while offensive and defensive teams collaborated to share detection logic with resource-constrained public sector bodies.

Key Takeaways:
Organizational culture serves as a vital defensive control; organizations must replace blame-oriented security metrics with supportive reporting environments that minimize incident detection latencies. Hiring managers should broaden recruitment criteria beyond traditional academic degrees and technical interrogations, prioritizing problem-solving abilities, high trust, and crisis-management experience. Breaking down internal departmental silos and incentivizing collective operational milestones fosters operational agility, higher employee retention, and more resilient defense postures.
